Search Engines 101

A search engine answers a query by first building an inverted index: a mapping from every term in the corpus to the documents that contain it. Without this structure, answering "which documents mention python" would mean scanning every document at query time, which does not scale past a handful of pages.

Once the index exists, relevance scoring takes over. The classic algorithm for this is BM25, which combines term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization into a single score per candidate document.

Building a real search engine from scratch touches crawling, boilerplate removal, indexing, compression, ranking, and distributed serving — each one a project in its own right.

Compressing Postings Lists

An uncompressed inverted index stores every document id as a full-width integer, even though postings are sorted by ascending document id and the gaps between consecutive ids are usually small. Delta encoding exploits exactly that: store the gap, not the absolute id.

Combined with a variable-length integer encoding like varint, and block-based bitpacking for the longest postings lists, this is what lets a real inverted index scale to millions of documents without postings dominating disk and memory.

Random access matters too: decoding one term's postings should never require reading the rest of the index.
